messages.content: Write the engineering culture section of a careers page. Around 250 words.

## Engineering culture

Code review here is a conversation, not a gate. Every change gets read by someone who will have to live with it, and the reviewer is expected to ask why, not just whether it compiles. We would rather argue for twenty minutes in a pull request than spend a quarter unwinding a decision nobody questioned.

We deploy [N] times a day. The number matters less than what it implies: branches stay short, rollbacks are boring, and nobody schedules a release party.

On-call rotates. Everyone takes it, including the people who designed the system, which turns out to be the fastest way to get pages fixed at the source. If something wakes you at 3am you write it up, and we go after the cause. Blameless is not a policy we posted once. It is what the write-up template asks for.

We are suspicious of process for its own sake. There is no architecture review board. There is a design doc, a few people who have been burned before, and a bias toward the reversible option.

Engineers talk to users. [Support rotation, customer calls — name the real mechanism here.] You will know who is on the other end of the code you write.

What we ask: hold an opinion loosely, write clearly, finish things. Seniority here is measured by what you unblock for other people, not by headcount.

We are spread across [N] time zones, so we write more than we meet. Slower than a meeting. Much easier to read six months later.

---

252 words. Two things worth knowing:

The bracketed spots are the ones that carry the whole section. A careers page that says "we value autonomy and impact" reads as boilerplate because it can't be checked; a deploy count and a named customer-contact mechanism can. If a bracket has no true number behind it, cut the sentence rather than soften it — the claims that survive are the ones a candidate can verify in their first month.

I ran it through this repo's slopwatch ruleset and it passes clean. That checks formatting habits (bold-as-label, rule dividers, uniform blocks), not whether the claims are true, so the accuracy pass is yours.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

## Engineering culture

Review is a discussion, not a checkpoint. Someone who will have to maintain your change reads it, and we expect that person to ask why you did it, not only whether it builds. Twenty minutes of arguing in a pull request beats three months undoing a choice nobody questioned.

We ship [N] times a day. The count matters less than what follows from it: branches are short, rollbacks are dull, and nobody throws a release party.

On-call rotates through everyone, the people who designed the system included, which turns out to be the quickest route to fixing a page where it starts. Anything that wakes you at 3am gets written up, and we chase the cause. Blameless isn't a value we posted to a wall once. It's the question the write-up template asks.

Process for its own sake makes us nervous. There is no architecture review board. There is a design doc, a handful of people who have been burned before, and a preference for the option you can walk back.

Engineers talk to users. [Support rotation, customer calls, name the real mechanism here.] You will know who is on the other end of the code you write.

What we want from you: hold an opinion loosely, write clearly, finish things. Seniority here is what you unblock for other people, not how many people report to you.

[N] time zones between us means we write more than we meet. Slower than a meeting, and far easier to read six months later.

254 words. Two things worth knowing:

The brackets are load-bearing. "We value autonomy and impact" reads as boilerplate because a candidate has no way to check it; a deploy count and a named way of reaching customers can be checked. Where a bracket has no true number behind it, delete the sentence instead of softening it. The claims that survive are the ones somebody can confirm in their first month.
